drills.title: DV01 of a 10-year position
drills.question: You hold $10 million face of a 10-year note priced at 96.00 with modified duration 8.12. What is the position DV01, and the approximate loss if yields rise 25 bp?
drills.solution: DV01 = market value x D_mod x 0.0001 = $9,600,000 x 8.12 x 0.0001 = $7,795.20 per bp. Loss = 25 x 7,795.20 = $194,880. Convexity would reduce the loss by roughly 0.5 x 78 x 0.0025^2 = 0.024% of value (about $2,300), so the duration figure is slightly high.
common_mistakes: Using face ($10m) instead of market value ($9.6m): gives $8,120
Multiplying by 0.01 instead of 0.0001 (confusing 1% with 1 bp)
drills.intuition: DV01 is duration expressed in dollars per basis point; it scales with market value, not face.
drills.takeaway: Memorize: a 10-year note near par has a DV01 near $780 per $1 million face.

drills.title: Bill discount rate to price, BEY and effective yield
drills.question: A 26-week (182-day) Treasury bill is quoted at a 4.00% discount rate. Compute its price per 100, its bond-equivalent yield, and its effective annual yield.
drills.solution: Price = 100(1 - 0.04 x 182/360) = 97.9778. BEY = (100 - 97.9778)/97.9778 x 365/182 = 4.1393%. Effective = (100/97.9778)^(365/182) - 1 = 4.1822%. The discount rate understates the investment return by about 14 bp because it divides by face and uses a 360-day year.
common_mistakes: Treating the 4.00% discount rate as the yield
Using 360 days in the BEY
Dividing the discount by face instead of price in the BEY
drills.intuition: Bills are quoted the way a banker discounts a note, not the way an investor measures return.
drills.takeaway: Convert every money-market quote to the same basis before comparing it with a note or a mortgage.

drills.title: Name the curve move and give two readings

inputs.context: day of a central bank meeting

drills.question: On the day of a central bank meeting the 2-year Treasury yield rises 30 bp and the 10-year rises 5 bp. Name the move. Give two economic interpretations and the data that would distinguish them. What does it mean for a floating-rate CRE borrower versus a fixed-rate borrower refinancing in five years?

rubric: Names it correctly: a bear flattener (yields up, short end more); 2s10s narrows 25 bp
Interpretation 1: the policy path was repriced higher (hawkish surprise); check fed funds futures and OIS for the change in expected rates
Interpretation 2: the market believes tighter policy now lowers long-run inflation or growth, so long-term expectations or the term premium fell; check breakevens and real yields at 10 years
Notes that the split between expectations and term premium is model-dependent
CRE: floating-rate borrower faces higher near-term debt service immediately; the five-year refinancer's base rate (5- to 10-year) moved much less, though cap rates may respond to credit conditions

drills.solution: A bear flattener. Either the policy path rose (front end) while long-run inflation expectations or the term premium fell (long end), or long-end buyers absorbed supply. Distinguish with OIS/futures changes, 10-year breakevens versus real yields, and published term-premium estimates (state the model). Floating borrowers feel the 30 bp now; fixed borrowers refinancing in five years face a base rate that barely moved.
common_mistakes: Calling it a steepener because yields rose
Assuming the long end must follow the short end
drills.intuition: The front end prices policy; the long end prices the average of policy plus a premium.
drills.takeaway: Read curve moves by tenor and map each tenor to the exposure it controls in your book.

drills.title: Size a DV01-neutral steepener
drills.question: You short $40 million face of the 10-year (DV01 0.0790 per 100) and buy the 2-year (DV01 0.0190 per 100) to be DV01-neutral. What 2-year face do you buy, what is the DV01 of each leg, and what is the approximate P&L if the 2-year falls 20 bp and the 10-year rises 5 bp? Name one risk the DV01 match does not remove.

rubric: Short convexity: loses on large parallel moves either way
Financing and repo specialness of the short 10-year
Gross notional and balance-sheet/margin limits
Exposure to other curve points (e.g., a 5-year twist)

drills.solution: 10-year leg DV01 = 40,000,000 x 0.0790/100 = $31,600 per bp. 2-year face = 31,600 / 0.000190 = $166.3 million (ratio 4.16). The 2s10s spread widens 5 - (-20) = 25 bp, so P&L is about 25 x 31,600 = +$790,000 before convexity and financing.
common_mistakes: Matching face instead of DV01
Getting the sign wrong: a steepener gains when the long yield rises relative to the short yield
drills.intuition: DV01 neutrality removes first-order exposure to parallel moves and leaves the spread.
drills.takeaway: Always report the trade's convexity and financing alongside its DV01.

drills.title: Decompose a cap-rate spread
drills.question: A property trades at a 6.25% cap rate. The 10-year Treasury yields 4.25%. Expected NOI growth after reserves is 2.5%. What is the cap-rate spread, and what unlevered risk premium does it imply?
drills.solution: Spread = 6.25 - 4.25 = 200 bp. From c = r_f + RP - g: RP = 6.25 + 2.50 - 4.25 = 4.50%. Required unlevered return = 8.75%.
common_mistakes: Reading the 200 bp spread as the risk premium (it is RP minus g)
Ignoring growth
drills.intuition: The spread is what is left of the risk premium after expected growth.
drills.takeaway: Never compare a spread with its history without asking whether growth or risk appetite changed.

drills.title: Refinancing a loan that no longer fits
drills.question: A suburban office property's maturing loan has a $22,000,000 balance. NOI after reserves is $1,800,000 and the appraiser uses a 7.00% cap rate. A lender offers 7.25% on 30-year amortization, max 65% LTV and min 1.30x DSCR. Compute value, the loan constant, the maximum loan, the refinancing gap, and the DSCR the existing balance would have at the new rate. What are the owner's options?

rubric: Identifies LTV as binding (DSCR test allows $16.91m)
Notes the existing balance would not even cover debt service at the new rate (DSCR about 1.00x)
Lists options: equity paydown, preferred equity or mezzanine, extension with paydown, discounted payoff, deed-in-lieu
Questions the 7.00% cap and the NOI: office leasing risk and capex may make both optimistic

common_mistakes: Sizing on DSCR only and missing that LTV binds
Using the interest rate instead of the loan constant
Ignoring that the appraisal cap may itself be stale
drills.intuition: At refinancing, the rate shock arrives through two doors at once: lower value (LTV) and a higher constant (DSCR).
drills.takeaway: Compute the gap before the maturity year, while options (extension, partial paydown, sale) are still cheap.

drills.title: Carry, roll and breakeven on a 2-year note
drills.question: You buy a 2-year note with a 4.00% coupon at par and finance it in repo at 4.30%. The 1.5-year par yield is 3.85%. Over six months, curve unchanged, compute carry, roll-down, total per 100 face, and the breakeven yield rise. Is this a carry trade?
drills.solution: Carry = 4.00 x 0.5 - 100 x 4.30% x 0.5 = 2.00 - 2.15 = -0.15. At the horizon the note is a 1.5-year 4.00% bond priced at 3.85%: 100.2166, so roll-down = +0.2166. Total = +0.0666. Horizon DV01 = 0.014462, so breakeven = 0.0666/0.014462 = 4.6 bp. It is not a carry trade: carry is negative and a 5 bp rise wipes out the total.
common_mistakes: Ignoring financing
Calling roll-down 'carry'
Using today's DV01 instead of the horizon DV01
drills.intuition: Roll-down pays only if the curve stays put; carry pays only if funding is cheaper than the coupon.
drills.takeaway: State the breakeven move with every carry argument.

drills.title: The cheap-spread pitch with contradictory evidence

inputs.cap_rate_source: appraisal-based index, last updated 2 quarters ago
inputs.transactions_last_quarter: very few; two sales, one distressed
inputs.financing: lenders quoting, but terms not yet indicated for this asset

drills.question: A broker argues that a property type is 'cheap' because its cap-rate/Treasury spread is 120 bp above its 10-year average. The cap rates come from an appraisal-based index last updated two quarters ago; there were two sales last quarter, one distressed; growth forecasts range from +4% (brokers) to -1% (independent research); and you have no financing terms for the asset. What is your recommendation?

rubric: Best answer is to abstain from a firm view or bid for now and specify the information to obtain
Explains that a wide spread can mean a high risk premium (cheap) or low expected growth (fair) and that the data cannot distinguish them
Flags appraisal lag and a thin, distressed-contaminated transaction sample as unreliable price evidence
Names the decisive data: transaction cap rates on arm's-length sales, lease rollover and market rent evidence, lender sizing terms
States what would change the answer: several arm's-length trades confirming cap rates, financing at a quoted DSCR and rate, growth evidence converging

drills.solution: Abstain. Spread = RP - g. With growth forecasts spanning five percentage points, the same spread is consistent with a risk premium from about 'cheap' to 'expensive'. The cap-rate data are stale and the transaction sample is two trades, one forced. Without financing terms you cannot even compute the refinancing exposure. The professional answer is a list of information to buy, with a date to revisit, not a trade.
common_mistakes: Treating the 10-year average as fair value
Treating appraisal cap rates as transaction prices
Averaging broker and independent forecasts without asking why they differ
drills.intuition: When the inputs to RP - g are both unknown, the spread is not a signal.
drills.takeaway: Abstention plus a specific information plan is a decision, and often the best one.

drills.title: Duration plus convexity for a 150 bp move
drills.question: A bond has modified duration 7.0 and convexity 60. Estimate the percentage price change for a 150 bp rise, first with duration only and then with convexity.
common_mistakes: Squaring 150 instead of 0.015
Subtracting the convexity term for a yield rise (it is always added for option-free bonds)
drills.intuition: Convexity cushions losses and boosts gains; it grows with the square of the move.
drills.takeaway: For stress moves of 150 bp or more, include convexity or reprice.

drills.title: IC case: lock the refinancing rate or not

inputs.context: hotel loan matures in one year; NOI recovering; sponsor wants to lock a forward-starting hedge

drills.question: A hotel owner must refinance a $30 million loan in one year. The annually compounded Treasury zero curve is 1-year 4.50%, 2-year 4.30%. The sponsor proposes locking the one-year rate one year forward with a forward-starting swap. Compute the implied 1-year rate one year forward. Then prepare an investment-committee recommendation: lock, buy an option (swaption or cap), or stay open.

rubric: Computes the forward correctly and notes it is below spot because the curve is inverted: the market prices cuts
Explains that locking the forward gives up the benefit if cuts exceed what is priced, and pays any term premium embedded in the forward
Ties hedge size to the refinancing balance and to the probability the refinancing happens as planned (sale, recapitalization or paydown would leave a naked swap)
Compares a lock with an option: the option costs premium but does not create a liability if rates fall
Addresses credit spread risk: the hedge covers the base rate only; hotel loan spreads may widen in a downturn
States what would change the decision: lender term sheet, NOI trajectory, the sponsor's liquidity to post collateral on a swap

drills.solution: f(1,2) = 1.043^2/1.045 - 1 = 4.1004%. The forward is about 40 bp below the 1-year spot, so the market already prices lower rates. A forward-starting swap locks the base rate near 4.10% but creates a liability if rates fall further and requires collateral; it hedges only the Treasury/swap component, not the hotel spread. Because the refinancing may be replaced by a sale or recapitalization, a cap or payer swaption sized to the balance is usually the better fit unless the lender requires a swap and the sponsor has liquidity for margin.
common_mistakes: Treating the forward as the expected rate (it contains a premium)
Hedging the full balance when the refinancing is uncertain
Forgetting that a swap's mark-to-market can require cash before the refinancing date
drills.intuition: A forward lock removes the base-rate uncertainty and replaces it with a contingent liability.
drills.takeaway: Hedge the exposure you will certainly have, with an instrument whose worst case you can fund.
